steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.

builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: BUMP: Brief Unexpected Mid-Interpolation Peak
summary: Replaces plain logit (prediction-space) ensembling of permutation-aligned model pairs with a hybrid scheme that also mixes weights near the interpolation endpoints, exploiting the brief accuracy peaks (BUMP) found there. Costs are modest: it requires at least two permutation-aligned models trained or fine-tuned from a shared init, plus endpoint weight interpolation and combined prediction mixing, adding storage for extra checkpoints and a small amount of offline search over interpolation coefficients. It can fail when models are not permutation-aligned (the peak depends on alignment), when the architecture or task falls outside the studied regimes, or when the near-endpoint gain does not survive the reader's specific data distribution, making the benefit workload-dependent.
rationale: The method is cheap to implement on constrained infrastructure but its accuracy and calibration gains are empirical and must be validated on the reader's own model pairs and data before production adoption.

claims.statement: Replaces plain logit (prediction-space) ensembling of permutation-aligned model pairs with a hybrid scheme that also mixes weights near the interpolation endpoints, exploiting the brief accuracy peaks (BUMP) found there. Costs are modest: it requires at least two permutation-aligned models trained or fine-tuned from a shared init, plus endpoint weight interpolation and combined prediction mixing, adding storage for extra checkpoints and a small amount of offline search over interpolation coefficients. It can fail when models are not permutation-aligned (the peak depends on alignment), when the architecture or task falls outside the studied regimes, or when the near-endpoint gain does not survive the reader's specific data distribution, making the benefit workload-dependent.
Consistently outperforms standard logit ensembling in test accuracy and yields improved calibration trade-off across the paper's experiments; no single multiplicative factor is reported.
